query: Geometry-Aware Probabilistic Circuits A natural way to equip PCs with geometry awareness is to replace the constant (global) sum node weights with geometry-aware gating, so that different expert subcircuits specialize to different regions of the data manifold. Voronoi tessellations (Aurenhammer, 1991) provide a principled mechanism for such routing. Formally, given centroids {c1, . . . , cK} ⊂ R d , what is the Voronoi cell of ck is defined as?
answer:
The evidence provided does not contain information directly related to Geometry-Aware Probabilistic Circuits or Voronoi tessellations. The MNEMOS_EVIDENCE focuses on separable neural architectures and their applications, particularly in KHRONOS for predictive and generative intelligence.

To address your query about the definition of a Voronoi cell:

Given centroids \(\{c_1, c_2, ..., c_K\} \subset \mathbb{R}^d\), the Voronoi cell \(V(c_k)\) of centroid \(c_k\) is defined as:
\[ V(c_k) = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^d : \|x - c_k\| \leq \|x - c_j\|, \forall j \neq k\} \]

This means that the Voronoi cell \(V(c_k)\) consists of all points in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) which are closer to centroid \(c_k\) than to any other centroid \(c_j\) for \(j \neq k\).

For a more detailed explanation and further reading, you might want to refer to computational geometry literature or specific works on Voronoi diagrams [1].

[1] Aurenhammer, F. (1991). "Voronoi Diagrams - A Survey of a Fundamental Geometric Data Structure." ACM Computing Surveys, 23(3), 345-405.
